title: THE OFFER THAT MADE AN APOSTLE TREMBLE: THE WARNING HIDDEN IN SIMON THE SORCERER’S MONEY
paragraphs: THE OFFER THAT MADE AN APOSTLE TREMBLE: THE WARNING HIDDEN IN SIMON THE SORCERER’S MONEY

He thought the power of God could be obtained through a transaction. Peter’s answer exposes something far more frightening than ancient sorcery: the hidden desire to possess what was only meant to be received by grace.

There is a sentence in the book of Acts that should make every Christian who has ever wanted influence, recognition, spiritual authority, ministry success, a platform, a title, a following—or even the appearance of being close to God—stop and examine the heart.
It begins with money in a man’s hand.
But the real scandal was happening somewhere much deeper.
Simon had seen something extraordinary.

He had watched the apostles lay their hands upon believers, and he witnessed the manifestation of the Holy Spirit’s work. Whatever Simon saw was powerful enough that the former magician immediately wanted access to it.
And then he made the offer.
Acts 8:18–19 records:

“Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, ‘Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.’”
At first glance, someone might almost misunderstand him.
Perhaps Simon simply wanted to serve.
Perhaps he wanted to help people.
Perhaps he wanted to participate in what God was doing.
Perhaps he was merely enthusiastic.
But Peter did not respond to the appearance of Simon’s request.
Peter went after the heart underneath it.
And what Peter said was terrifying.
The Greek text of Acts 8:20 begins:
“Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν…”
To argyrion sou syn soi eiē eis apōleian…
“May your silver perish with you…”
Why?
“ὅτι τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνόμισας διὰ χρημάτων κτᾶσθαι.”
Hoti tēn dōrean tou Theou enomisas dia chrēmatōn ktasthai.
“…because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money.”
There it is.
The warning hidden inside Simon’s offer.
Simon saw a gift…
and imagined a transaction.
God was giving.
Simon was thinking about acquiring.
God was pouring out grace.
Simon was calculating access.
The apostles were servants through whom God was working.
Simon wanted the power associated with their hands.
And suddenly this story stops feeling ancient.
Because Simon may be dead…
but Simon’s temptation is not.
It can walk into churches.
It can stand behind pulpits.
It can sit behind microphones.
It can open ministry pages.
It can publish books.
It can build Christian brands.
It can chase titles.
It can count followers.
It can obsess over engagement.
It can envy another believer’s influence.
It can secretly dream about being called “anointed.”
And sometimes it can kneel during worship while quietly asking a question the mouth would never dare say aloud:
“What can Christianity give me?”
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because you do not need to practice sorcery to share Simon’s temptation.
You only need to want the things of God more than you want God Himself.
Simon’s story begins earlier in Acts 8.
Before Philip arrived in Samaria preaching Christ, Simon had practiced magic and astonished the people. Acts tells us that he presented himself as someone great, and people paid attention to him.
That detail matters.
Simon knew what it felt like to have people watching.
He knew influence.
He knew attention.
He knew what it was like when a crowd associated his name with extraordinary power.
Then Philip arrived.
And everything changed.
Philip did not preach Philip.
Acts 8:5 says:
“Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.”
Christ.
Not personal greatness.
Not celebrity.
Not spiritual branding.
Christ.
The crowds who had been amazed by Simon began paying attention to the Gospel.
People believed.
People were baptized.
Lives were changing.
And remarkably, Acts 8:13 says that Simon himself believed and was baptized, continuing with Philip and being amazed at the signs and great miracles he witnessed.
Then Peter and John arrived.
And Simon saw something he had never possessed.
Something money could not manufacture.
Something technique could not reproduce.
Something reputation could not create.
Something sorcery could not imitate into existence.
The work of the living God.
And the old instinct surfaced.
Acquire it.
Possess it.
Get access to it.
“Give me this power also…”
Those words expose one of the oldest corruptions of religion:
wanting God’s power without surrendering to God’s ownership.
And Peter refuses to entertain it.
He tells Simon:
“You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.”
Notice where Peter points.
Not Simon’s wallet.
His heart.
“ἡ γὰρ καρδία σου οὐκ ἔστιν εὐθεῖα ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ.”
Hē gar kardia sou ouk estin eutheia enanti tou Theou.
“For your heart is not right before God.”
That is the diagnosis.
Simon’s money merely revealed what his heart believed.
And money still does that.
Influence still does that.
Ambition still does that.
Success still does that.
The desire to be noticed still does that.
They expose us.
There is nothing inherently sinful about money. Scripture does not teach that possessing money is itself evil. Paul says in 1 Timothy 6:10 that “the love of money” is a root of all kinds of evils.
There is nothing inherently sinful about having influence either. God gave influence to Joseph, Daniel, Esther, Peter, Paul, and many others.
The question is what happens inside us when influence becomes available.
Do we want people to see Jesus?
Or do we secretly need them to see us standing near Jesus?
There is a difference.
A devastating one.
You can speak about Christ while building yourself.
You can serve people while craving their admiration.
You can give generously while secretly wanting recognition.
You can know biblical vocabulary while your heart is negotiating with God.
You can even want spiritual gifts for selfish reasons.
And perhaps one of the most frightening possibilities is that other people may never notice.
But Jesus does.
This is why Simon’s story should not primarily become ammunition for accusing somebody else.
It should become a mirror.
Before you think about the preacher you distrust…
the ministry you criticize…
the Christian influencer you suspect…
the wealthy religious leader who irritates you…
look inward.
Ask the harder question.
“Lord, is Simon hiding anywhere in me?”
Would I still serve if nobody applauded?
Would I still give if nobody knew?
Would I still pray if nobody heard me?
Would I still worship if there were no emotional reward?
Would I still obey if obedience cost me followers?
Would I still preach Christ if somebody else received the recognition?
Would I still love Jesus if He never made me impressive?
That last question hurts.
Because there is a version of Christianity that can quietly turn Jesus into a means of obtaining something else.
Jesus for success.
Jesus for money.
Jesus for influence.
Jesus for relationships.
Jesus for healing.
Jesus for status.
Jesus for an audience.
Jesus for a better life.
And yes, God gives good gifts.
He provides.
He heals according to His will.
He restores.
He opens doors.
He blesses His children in countless ways.
But Christianity is not ultimately about using Jesus to obtain the treasure.
Jesus is the treasure.
Paul could say in Philippians 3:8 that he counted everything as loss because of “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.”
Not merely knowing what Jesus could provide.
Knowing Jesus.
Simon wanted power.
Peter called him to repentance.
Acts 8:22:
“Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.”
The Greek begins:
“μετανόησον οὖν…”
Metanoēson oun…
“Repent, therefore…”
That word matters.
Repentance is not image management.
It is not learning how to hide your sin more effectively.
It is not changing vocabulary while protecting the idol.
Biblical repentance involves turning from sin toward God.
Peter does not tell Simon to improve his personal brand.
He does not tell him to make a larger donation.
He does not offer Simon a premium level of apostolic power.
He tells him to repent.
That destroys every attempt to turn the Gospel into merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased because grace, by definition, is gift.
The Greek word Peter uses in Acts 8:20 is dōrea—gift.
“The gift of God.”
Simon’s fundamental mistake was trying to place a price tag on what God called gift.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity really does involve a transaction—but not the transaction Simon imagined.
You do not purchase salvation from God.
You could never afford it.
Your morality cannot purchase it.
Your church attendance cannot purchase it.
Your donations cannot purchase it.
Your tears cannot purchase it.
Your ministry cannot purchase it.
Your suffering cannot purchase it.
Your reputation cannot purchase it.
Your followers cannot purchase it.
Your religious achievements cannot purchase it.
Someone else paid.
Jesus Christ.
Peter himself would later write:
Not silver.
Not gold.
Blood.
His blood.
The Son of God did what Simon’s money could never do.
Christ stepped into the place of sinners.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not say, “Bring enough and God might accept you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves, and calls us to repent and believe.
That is why grace humiliates human pride before it heals the human heart.
You arrive empty-handed.
The rich arrive empty-handed.
The poor arrive empty-handed.
The famous arrive empty-handed.
The forgotten arrive empty-handed.
The pastor arrives empty-handed.
The addict arrives empty-handed.
The successful businessman arrives empty-handed.
The broken mother arrives empty-handed.
The ashamed teenager arrives empty-handed.
The prisoner arrives empty-handed.
The religious person arrives empty-handed.
The person who ruined everything arrives empty-handed.
And at the foot of the cross there is no VIP line.
Only sinners who need mercy.
Maybe that is why this story found you.
Maybe you have been performing.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make God impressed with you.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you are from trying to appear spiritually strong.
Maybe your prayers have quietly become negotiations.
“God, if I do this, will You give me that?”
“God, if I serve You, will You make my life easier?”
“God, if I give, will You owe me?”
“God, if I obey, will You make people recognize me?”
And when God did not follow the script…
you became angry.
Because somewhere along the way, surrender became a contract.
Simon’s story whispers across the centuries:
God cannot be bought.
But the Gospel shouts something even better:
You do not need to buy Him.
Christ invites sinners to come.
Maybe you have failed badly.
Maybe your motives have been polluted.
Maybe pride has been hiding underneath ministry.
Maybe greed has been hiding underneath ambition.
Maybe you wanted the platform more than the presence of God.
Maybe you wanted people impressed with your Christianity more than you wanted Christ transforming your character.
Do not run from Jesus because the truth exposed you.
Run toward Him.
Conviction is not an invitation to pretend harder.
It is an invitation to repent.
There is grace for the exposed.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is cleansing for sinners.
There is restoration for people who finally stop defending what God is trying to remove.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin was never serious.
He rewrites everything because He took sin so seriously that He carried its judgment at the cross.
Grace is not God saying sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
So examine your heart.
Not your image.
Not your profile.
Not your reputation.
Your heart.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to manufacture a spiritual answer. Tell Christ the truth.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
Your confession may become somebody else’s courage.
And do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Let them discover Jesus.
Because Simon’s temptation does not disappear after one reading.
Success can resurrect it.
Recognition can resurrect it.
Money can resurrect it.
Ministry growth can resurrect it.
Even answered prayer can reveal motives we did not know were hiding inside us.
Come back and read this when your heart begins confusing being used by God with being admired by people.
It does not.
Not because supporting this ministry earns salvation.
It cannot.
Not because God needs your money before He can work.
He does not.
Simon’s story should make us extremely careful never to communicate anything like that.
If you want to glorify God through your resources, do so first by surrendering those resources to His lordship and using them faithfully, generously, and without compulsion.
Simon reached for his money because he misunderstood the gift.
Do not repeat his mistake in another form.
You cannot purchase the Holy Spirit.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot purchase the favor of God.
You cannot purchase spiritual authority.
You cannot purchase a place at the cross.
You cannot purchase the blood of Jesus.
You come empty-handed.
You repent.
You believe.
You receive grace.
And then, because grace has changed you, you begin living differently.
Giving differently.
Serving differently.
Leading differently.
Loving differently.
You stop asking, “How can I use God to become somebody?”
And begin praying:
“Jesus, even if nobody remembers my name, let my life make them remember Yours.”
That is freedom.
Simon wanted power in his hands.
Jesus wants surrender in your heart.
Simon offered silver.
Jesus offered Himself.
Simon wanted something he could possess.
The Gospel gives us a Savior before whom we gladly surrender possession of ourselves.
So the next time ambition whispers that you need a platform…
the next time comparison tells you someone else has more spiritual influence…
the next time money tempts you to believe everything has a price…
the next time you secretly crave the appearance of anointing more than the holiness produced through abiding in Christ…
remember the silver in Simon’s hand.
Remember Peter’s warning.
Remember the cross.
And remember that the greatest gift God gives sinners cannot be bought because the price has already been paid by Someone else.
If this article exposed you, comment.
Because someday, every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes irrelevant.
Every title is laid down.
Every bank account is left behind.
Every human name eventually fades from somebody’s memory.
And when all the silver finally slips from our hands, only one question will matter:
Did we want what Jesus could give us…
or did we finally realize that Jesus Himself was everything?
You were never meant to purchase the fire of God—you were meant to lay your life on the altar and belong completely to Christ.
